newsitem.title: USA: Contempt threat for former administration aides.
newsitem.headline: Contempt threat for former administration aides.

text.p: The chairman of a House committee investigating campaign fund-raising said Friday he would seek contempt charges against two former administration officials if they refuse to turn over subpoenaed documents.

Webster Hubbell, a former associate attorney general, and former Commerce Department official John Huang wrote the House Government Reform Committee this week that they were invoking their constitutional right against possible self-incrimination and would not comply with committee subpoenas.

"We're moving forward to compel a full and complete response to the committee's subpoenas for documents from Mr. Huang and Mr. Hubbell. We are pursuing all legal channels in our attempt to obtain these subpoenaed records," Chairman Dan Burton, an Indiana Republican, said in a statement.

Burton said if Huang and Hubbell continued to defy the subpoenas, he would schedule a committee vote to find them in contempt of Congress, a charge which could send both to jail if they were found guilty in court.
Hubbell was a long time friend of President Clinton and was a law partner of Hillary Rodham Clinton at the Rose law firm in Little Rock, Arkansas, before Clinton was elected.

Huang raised funds for the Democratic party from Asian-Americans after he left the Commerce Department. Almost half of the $3.4 million he brought in has since been returned by the party because of questions about its sources.

"We are not prepared to negotiate over these documents," Burton said. "Disturbing new allegations are coming to light every week. I am deeply troubled that former senior administration officials have refused to cooperate with this investigation."
Burton said Huang has turned over some documents but Hubbell has refused to turn over any.
White House spokesman Mike McCurry said Clinton had had no recent contact with Hubble but thought witnesses ought to cooperate.

"We're not in a position to understand their individual pursuit of their own rights in representations they are making to the committee, so we have no comment," McCurry said. "The president has always urged people to cooperate."

Clinton has said mistakes were made in Democratic fund-raising activities but said he knew nothing about it. He called for investigations of the fund-raising and urged Congress to pass campaign finance reform legislation.

The Senate Governmental Affairs Committee was also investigating the fund-raising activities and hearings by both committees were expected later this year. The Justice Department was conducting its own investigation.
The House and Senate committees are both headed by Republicans and Democrats have called on them to be even-handed and investigate Republican fund-raising too.

New York Sen. Daniel Patrick Moynihan became the first Democrat to call for the appointment of an independent counsel to investigate the matter, saying Tuesday he was concerned about the possibility of foreign involvement.

Attorney General Janet Reno has so far refused requests for an independent counsel. The independent counsel law was passed after the Watergate scandal to ensure impartial investigations of executive branch officials.
